title: Building Recurring Revenue
summary: Clear sign-up date → Billed on repeat → Steady income, honestly earned
subtitle: Turn one-time jobs into steady income that customers are glad to keep.

blocks.text: Recurring revenue is money that comes in on a set schedule, such as a monthly retainer, a membership or a yearly service plan. It makes a small business calmer, because you can count on next month’s income instead of hoping for it. This lesson shows you how to build it honestly, so customers stay because they want to.
Build income that arrives every month, without trapping anyone to get it.
blocks.detail: A clear plan and an honest renewal process give you steady income and customers who recommend you. That is worth more than a long contract nobody likes.
blocks.extra: Section 03 explains how to design a plan and which rules apply.

blocks.text: A one-time sale pays you once, and then you must find the next customer. A recurring sale pays you again each month or year for as long as the customer stays. Common examples are a monthly cleaning plan, a bookkeeping retainer, a seasonal lawn service, a coaching membership and a subscription box.

Two numbers matter most: monthly recurring revenue and churn. Monthly recurring revenue is the total you expect to bill each month. Churn is the share of customers who cancel in a month. It tells you how well your service keeps people.
Recurring income still takes work. You deliver the service every month, so the plan must be priced to cover your time as well as your costs.

items.title: MONTHLY RECURRING REVENUE
items.text: 31 customers × $90 a month = $2,790 you can expect to bill each month, before tax.

items.title: CHURN
items.text: 2 of 31 customers cancel this month. 2 ÷ 31 = about 6.5% churn.

items.title: WHY IT MATTERS
items.text: At 6.5% a month, you need about two new customers every month just to stay level. Lower churn means less time spent chasing new sales.

sections.title: Designing a plan, and the rules that apply

blocks.text: Start with a service customers already need on a regular basis. Bundle it into a simple monthly or yearly plan with a clear price, a clear list of what is included and a clear way to stop. Customers join plans that feel predictable and fair.

items.title: Retainer
list: How it works: A fixed monthly fee for an agreed amount of work
Example: A bookkeeper who reviews your accounts each month

items.title: Membership
list: How it works: A monthly fee for access to your content or community
Example: A fitness or hobby group

items.title: Service plan
list: How it works: A regular visit or delivery at a set price
Example: Lawn care, cleaning, or pet visits

items.title: Prepaid package
list: How it works: A larger payment up front for a bundle of sessions
Example: Ten tutoring hours at a small discount

blocks.text: Advertise the price people will pay. In June 2024, Sirius XM agreed to pay a $3.3 million penalty to settle Competition Bureau concerns that a required fee made its plans cost 10% to 20% more than the advertised price. A fixed fee everyone must pay belongs in the price you advertise. Government taxes are the usual exception.

items.title: “A free trial that renews automatically is just good business.”
items.text: The Competition Bureau warns about subscription traps, where people give card details for a free or cheap offer and end up locked into a monthly charge. Watch for pre-checked boxes, unclear cancellation terms and return policies that are hard to find. These practices damage trust and can break the law.

blocks.text: Provincial consumer protection laws also cover renewals and cancelling, and the rules differ across Canada. Before you launch, read the guidance from your province’s consumer protection office. Quebec’s consumer law has special rules for contracts with ongoing service, so check them with care if you sell in Quebec or market to Quebecers.

Put the terms where people can see them. State the price, the billing date, the renewal date and how to cancel, in plain words, before the customer pays. Email customers before each renewal, and make cancelling as easy as signing up.
Sales tax and records

Each billing is a taxable sale. Once you are registered for GST/HST, you charge tax on every payment and report it on your return. Keep a record of each customer, the start date, the price and every payment, because repeat billing creates many small records.

Prepaid money is a promise, not profit. When a customer pays for a year up front, you still owe them eleven months of work. Keep enough of it in reserve to deliver the rest of the plan, or to give back the unused part if you stop.

A chargeback costs more than a refund. If a customer can’t find a way to cancel, they may ask their card company to reverse the payment. A quick, polite refund for a renewal they didn’t want usually costs less than a dispute, and it protects your name.
The Fridge Calendar
paragraphs: Marisol Dubé ran a small lawn and snow-clearing business in Moncton. She kept a paper calendar on her fridge, and every slow month got a red X. Her goal was to cover her truck payments in January and February, when the calendar was nearly all red.

She decided to offer a year-round plan for $90 a month, plus HST. It covered lawn care in summer and snow clearing in winter. Fourteen neighbours signed up in the first month. Marisol watched the red Xs turn into green ticks and felt more hopeful than she had in a long time.

Then she hit a problem. A friend told her to tuck the auto-renewal into the fine print and make cancelling a little awkward, so people would forget and stay. The plan would renew each year with no reminder. Customers would have to phone during office hours to leave.

She faced a choice. She could take that advice and keep more customers on paper. Or she could send a clear email a month before each renewal, with a one-click link to cancel. She thought about her own phone bill and how much she hated feeling trapped. She chose the open way.

The result surprised her. A few customers did cancel, but far more stayed, and several wrote back to say the email made them trust her. Four of them told their neighbours. Within a year she had thirty-one plans.
Most of the red Xs vanished from the fridge calendar. Marisol made her truck payments that January without a worry, and in March she bought a second snow blower.

blocks.text: Honest renewals build the kind of customers who stay by choice.
blocks.detail: Clear terms and easy cancelling cost you a few customers, and win you far more referrals and a name that sells for you.
blocks.extra: Section 05 gives you a short launch plan for your own recurring offer.

items.title: Pick one recurring need.
items.text: Choose a service customers already buy again and again.

items.title: Write a simple plan.
items.text: List the price, what is included, how often you deliver it and how to cancel.

items.title: Price it to cover your time.
items.text: Use the steps from Pricing Services, and include every required fee in the advertised price.

items.title: Show the terms up front.
items.text: Show the billing date, renewal date and how to cancel before the customer pays.

items.title: Remind before you renew.
items.text: Email before each renewal, and make cancelling simple.

items.title: Track and report.
items.text: Record each payment, charge sales tax if you are registered and report the income on Form T2125.

blocks.text: Notes by province, and for your taxes

items.title: Sales tax
items.text: Rates differ across Canada, for example 5% GST in Alberta, 13% HST in Ontario and 15% HST in New Brunswick. Confirm the rate for your buyer’s location before you bill.

items.title: Consumer rules
items.text: Provincial laws on renewals and cancelling vary, so check your province’s consumer protection office.

items.title: Quebec
items.text: Quebec’s consumer law and French-language rules apply to offers aimed at Quebecers.

items.title: “Recurring revenue means I no longer have to look for new customers.”
items.text: Some customers always leave, because their needs change or they move. You still need a steady trickle of new customers to replace the ones who go.

blocks.text: Insider tip: Check your churn every month. If more than a few customers cancel, ask three of them why. Their answers show you what to fix, and they cost you nothing.
Quick Check

items.title: What is churn?
items.detail: The share of customers who cancel in a given period.

items.title: Does a mandatory monthly fee belong in the advertised price?
items.text: Only government taxes can be added later.

items.title: Do you charge GST/HST on each repeating payment?
items.text: once you are registered.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: Which is a sign of a subscription trap? A. Clear terms and a one-click cancel link · B. A pre-checked box and hidden cancellation steps · C. A reminder email before renewal
items.text: Hidden terms and hard cancellation are exactly what the Competition Bureau warns about.

items.title: A mandatory monthly service fee is charged to every customer. Where should it appear? A. Only in the terms and conditions · B. In the advertised price · C. On the final checkout page only
items.text: Mandatory fixed fees must be part of the price people see first.

items.title: What does a lower churn rate mean? A. More customers are staying · B. More customers are cancelling · C. Your prices are too low
items.text: Churn measures cancellations, so lower churn means that customers are staying longer.

items.title: In one sentence, describe the recurring plan you could offer.
items.text: A $90 monthly plan for lawn care in summer and snow clearing in winter, with a reminder email before each renewal.

blocks.text: Offer a clear plan, show the true price, remind before renewing, and make cancelling easy. Customers who stay by choice are worth more.

items.title: Recurring revenue
items.text: Income that arrives on a regular schedule.

items.title: Retainer
items.text: A fixed regular fee for an agreed amount of work.

items.title: Churn
items.text: The share of customers who cancel in a period.

items.title: Auto-renewal
items.text: A plan that keeps going unless the customer cancels.

items.title: Chargeback
items.text: A card payment reversed at the customer’s request to their card company.

items.title: Subscription trap
items.text: A free or cheap offer that locks a customer into regular charges.
